posts.title: HOW DO PEOPLE HACK PEOPLE'S CRYPTO WALLETS?
posts.author: MUSTAPHA MUSA
posts.snippet:
HOW DO PEOPLE HACK PEOPLE'S CRYPTO WALLETS?

There are several ways a scammer can gain access to your wallet and drain all the assets inside within a very short time. These methods include:

1. Exposing Your Seed Phrase

Many people store their seed phrases online, which is extremely risky. If a scammer gains access to your email account or the storage platform where you saved your seed phrase, it's game over. They can gain full access to your wallet without any difficulty.

Therefore, never share your seed phrase with anyone, regardless of who they claim to be. If you do, you may have no one to blame but yourself if your funds are stolen.

Scammers are everywhere, especially on Twitter (X), so always be vigilant.

2. Participating in Fake Airdrops

Some airdrop scams require you to connect your wallet to their website before you can claim the airdrop. Once you do, scammers may drain your wallet and leave you with nothing.

The best practice is to create a separate wallet specifically for participating in airdrops. Once you receive any rewards, transfer them to your main wallet.

Furthermore, whenever you connect your wallet to any website, make sure you understand what you're approving before proceeding. Check the type of connection or permission being requested. Is it merely an authentication request, or are you granting the website permission to move or access your assets?

Always be careful.

3. Viruses and Malware

It is advisable to install reliable antivirus software on your computer because malware can be used to steal sensitive information stored on your device, including information related to your crypto wallet. This could eventually lead to the loss of all your assets.

That is why you should avoid relying solely on cloud storage to keep your seed phrase. Instead, consider writing it down or printing it on paper and storing it in a secure location to minimize the risk of theft or unauthorized access.

Remember: Keeping your seed phrase offline and secure is one of the best ways to protect your wallet.

4. Greed and the Desire to Get Rich Quickly

I remember a scam that was popular around 2019–2020. People would receive unspendable Bitcoin in their Blockchain.com wallets, and they would be told that if they wanted to use the Bitcoin, they needed to provide their seed phrases to have their wallets activated.

Through this trick, many people were scammed and lost access to their funds.

Therefore, never let the desire to get rich overnight blind you to the risks of a deal that seems too good to be true. Never give your recovery phrase to anyone, no matter how convincing their offer may sound.

May God guide us and help us make the right decisions.

There are many ways scammers try to separate people from their hard-earned assets, so we must always remain vigilant.
FINAL WORD
In summary, never share your seed phrase or private keys with anyone. If you do and your funds are stolen, you may have no one to blame but yourself.

posts.title: The worst time to test your digital asset recovery plan is when you need it.
posts.author: CoinCover
posts.snippet:
The worst time to test your digital asset recovery plan is when you need it.

You can have the key material backed up, the policies documented, and the right people assigned. On paper, everything looks covered.

Then something goes wrong. The person with recovery authority has left. Your approval structure has changed. The process hasn’t been tested in months. Suddenly, the backup you were relying on isn’t the safety net you thought it was.

For financial institutions holding digital assets, having a backup and being able to recover are two very different things. Recovery infrastructure needs to work through staff changes, operational failures and high-pressure incidents — not just look good in a policy document.

See what financial institutions should look for when choosing crypto recovery infrastructure 👇

comments.text: The distinction worth stressing is between key backup and recovery authority - plenty of institutions have redundant key shares but no tested process for who can actually authorize their use under pressure, which is where incidents actually fail.
Do you find institutions test recovery authority changes (departures, role shifts) on a fixed schedule, or only after an incident forces the question?

We've seen forensic engagements stall for days simply because the person with signing authority had left the organisation and nobody had updated the approval chain - the documentation was fine, the people weren't.

posts.title: Personal accounts and corporate risk aren't as separate as most security policies make them appear.
posts.author: Guardian Digital Inc.
posts.snippet:
Personal accounts and corporate risk aren't as separate as most security policies make them appear.

An employee may access a crypto exchange from the same laptop used for Microsoft 365, cloud applications, internal communications, and customer systems.

If a phishing campaign progresses from credential theft to malware, the ownership of the original account becomes almost irrelevant.

The device is the bridge.

This is one reason endpoint visibility and identity telemetry matter even when the initial incident appears unrelated to company infrastructure.

Personal compromise can become enterprise exposure without crossing a neat administrative boundary.

#CyberSecurity #EndpointSecurity #SecurityOperations #RiskManagement
posts.reason: Solid discussion of device-level risk bridging personal and corporate security relevant to CISOs and risk officers, though not specifically crypto-focused enough for our strongest positioning.

comments.text: This is exactly the pattern we see in crypto-adjacent fraud cases - the initial compromise is a personal account, but the device's identity telemetry is what carries the exposure into corporate systems, which is why endpoint-level visibility matters more than account ownership.

Do your incident playbooks distinguish between a personal-account compromise that stays contained versus one that shows lateral movement toward corporate credentials, or is every flagged event treated the same initially?

In forensic work tracing funds from compromised personal crypto accounts, we regularly find the same device was used to access corporate cloud tools - the administrative line between personal and corporate was never really a technical one.

posts.title: Interpol published the results of Operation Serengeti III this week. Between the end of June and the end of August, police in 21 countries, South Africa among them, arrested 1,462
posts.author: Nihka Technology Group
posts.snippet:
Interpol published the results of Operation Serengeti III this week. Between the end of June and the end of August, police in 21 countries, South Africa among them, arrested 1,462 people, took down 10,909 malicious networks and recovered more than $105 million. Investigators identified almost 66,000 victims and traced losses of more than $385 million.

The cases read like a South African IT department’s inbox. In Nigeria, one suspect ran a phishing and business email compromise operation that had harvested around 2.1 million email addresses. In Uganda, two rings staffed by 365 foreign nationals ran fake trading platforms aimed at pensioners. In Tanzania, a loan app that stole from the phones it was installed on. In Angola, two illegal crypto-mining centres with their own stolen power supply. Ransomware and digital extortion are on the list too.

Two things are worth taking from it. These operations are run as businesses, with staff, premises and infrastructure, which is why one arrest rarely ends a campaign. And the recovered money is less than a third of the traced losses, which were themselves only the cases the police reached. The fake investment pitch, the supplier invoice with new bank details and the loan app on a staff member’s phone are being produced at industrial scale on this continent. Interpol took a slice out of it for two months.

#CyberSecurity #Interpol #Africa
posts.reason: Interpol operation addressing crypto fraud, ransomware and digital extortion at scale appeals to law enforcement and compliance buyers, though commentary would risk seeming opportunistic on a breaking case.

AI Under Legal Scrutiny | Episode 19
Your wallet is encrypted. But are you protected?
When we hear about cryptocurrency theft, we usually picture someone breaking into a system from behind a screen. Sharjah’s “End of Battle” operation revealed a much wider picture.
On 15 October 2026, Sharjah Police, working with the UAE Ministry of Interior, announced the dismantling of four interconnected international networks. According to the authorities, their activities included digital wallet theft, hacking, fraud, extortion, money laundering and violent assaults.
The announcement confirmed the use of artificial intelligence in those activities. The case involved 33 accused individuals and companies, with more than AED 200 million seized and confiscated.
The widely reported AED 65 billion figure refers to assets secured—not the amount stolen.
What interests me legally is the division of roles: one person obtains the data, another gains access to the wallet, and someone else moves the proceeds or conceals their origin. posts.title: An engineer scheduled a task on his employer's domain controller, went home, and let it run.
posts.author: Ironveil GRC
posts.snippet:
An engineer scheduled a task on his employer's domain controller, went home, and let it run.

Thirteen domain administrator accounts deleted. Passwords reset on 301 user accounts, 254 servers, and 3,284 workstations. Then the extortion email, with the subject line "Your Network Has Been Penetrated." Twenty bitcoin, or forty servers go dark every day for ten days.

He was sentenced to 32 months in federal prison in September 2026. The company never paid. What it did instead was correlate its own log timeline against physical badge-in records, and that is how the FBI ended up at a residential IP address in Warren County, New Jersey.

Insider risk is an access design problem, not a personality problem.
One role held enough privilege to lock out an entire enterprise. NIST 800-53 AC-5 and AC-6(9) have covered this for years. Most privileged access reviews count accounts and stop there. They never ask what a single account can actually reach.

Attackers are leaving AI artifacts in their own infrastructure.
CrowdStrike, investigating breaches across South Korea's financial sector, found Claude Code session histories and ARTEX configuration files sitting in the attacker's environment. Agent session files and memory files are evidence now. Check whether your IR playbook says who collects them.

Your build pipeline is a credential vault with a public contribution path.
Two open source maintainers lost their GitHub accounts, and a credential-stealing workflow went into more than 340 repositories. Socket then tracked over 500 accounts spreading it across tens of thousands more. A separate npm package shipped a worm that harvests npm, GitHub, AWS, Kubernetes, and Vault secrets on install. GV.SC in CSF 2.0 stopped being optional a while ago.

Backup platforms are a target, not a safety net.
Two AhsayCBS flaws, CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, were chained in early October 2026 to drop web shells and crypto miners on backup servers, before a patch existed. HIPAA 164.308(a)(7) asks for a backup plan and a disaster recovery plan. Code execution on the backup console defeats both in one move.

Pull your domain admin list before your next quarterly review. How many names are on it, and how many of those people still need to be?

Can you rob someone of bitcoin? Thailand's Supreme Court says yes.

Decision 4929/2569, decided in plenary, closes a gap defence lawyers had been testing: if cryptocurrency is not legal tender, is it "property" at all?

The facts. Five men cornered a couple in a café on Koh Samui, punched and threatened the husband, and made him convert USD 50,000 into bitcoin on his own phone and send it to their wallet. They left by van and motorbike. The defendant — the man who arranged the vehicles, the rooms and the ferry off the island — argued that nothing of value was taken: the Bank of Thailand itself says crypto is not legal tender, so no property, no robbery.

The court disagreed, on three grounds. The Digital Asset Decree defines cryptocurrency as an electronic data unit used as a medium of exchange. It has a market price, converts to cash and can be held by anyone. And digital-asset businesses trade it under SEC supervision. A coin "has form" on an electronic network, has a price and can be possessed. It is property under the Civil and Commercial Code, and taking it completes a property offence.

Conviction for gang robbery with a vehicle upheld through all three courts. Ten years. Return the bitcoin, or its baht value at the time of the transfer.

What it changes for compliance teams:

1. Every property offence now reaches coin — theft, extortion, fraud, embezzlement, robbery. Coin is no loophole.
2. Value is fixed at the moment of transfer, in fiat at that day's rate. Restitution in coin or baht.
3. The court read the forced fiat-to-crypto step as a move to hinder tracing. That is a typology: buy on own phone, sweep everything out to a new address, same session.

This transfer never touched a Thai-licensed operator. The next one might — and then the question is whether your monitoring saw a coerced transaction.

posts.title: A new infostealer doesn't just steal passwords — it steals your AI sessions.
posts.author: Omar Eldeeb
posts.snippet:
A new infostealer doesn't just steal passwords — it steals your AI sessions.

Check Point researchers found it and named it Aokigahara, after Japan's "haunted forest" at the base of Mount Fuji.

The target list is what makes it new. Alongside browsers, crypto wallets, VPN clients and password managers on Windows machines, it goes after Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot and Gemini CLI.

Not the apps themselves. The way in.

Aokigahara specifically collects authentication files, session data and configuration files tied to those AI tools.

Then it takes the rest of the keychain: Git access data, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure and Google Cloud configuration files.

It's built to stay hidden. It checks for virtual machines and sandboxes before it runs. Stolen data gets packed into zip archives, encrypted, and sent to attacker-controlled servers.

Suzu Labs CTO Denis Calderone put the stakes plainly: "a developer's AI assistant is a keyring."

The damage compounds from one machine. "The same malware that lifts the Cursor or Copilot session is also grabbing Git credentials, SSH private keys, and AWS config files off that workstation, so one infected machine can expose the codebase, the repos, and the cloud in a single run."

The money has changed too. A stolen AI session is a resellable paid subscription. It's also a conversation history full of proprietary code and business data.

That gives attackers a second lever: extortion value alongside resale value.

Which raises the question nobody has answered. If a session token unlocks a history full of proprietary source code, who owns protecting it — the AI vendor or the enterprise?

Right now, defenders assume neither.

Treat AI-tool authentication data as enterprise secrets, the same way you treat cloud keys. Hunt for suspicious access to local storage and auth files belonging to AI assistants and coding agents. Cut long-lived secrets off endpoints. Prefer managed identity and short-lived credentials.

And when an endpoint is suspected, Check Point's guidance is direct: assess AI sessions, API keys, GitHub credentials, SSH keys and cloud tokens — not just browser passwords.

Does your incident response playbook include AI session tokens yet — or does it still stop at browser passwords?

posts.title: We have submitted the Australian Bitcoin Industry Body's response to the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill 2026: Tax Information Reporting.
posts.author: Australian Bitcoin Industry Body
posts.snippet:
We have submitted the Australian Bitcoin Industry Body's response to the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill 2026: Tax Information Reporting.

Our concern goes beyond whether the proposed database can be secured. Is collecting this much information, at this level of detail and frequency, necessary and proportionate?

The financial case warrants scrutiny.

The Government's 2025–26 Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook forecasts for CARF and the proposed Domestic Crypto Reporting Regime (DCRR) combined:
• $170 million in additional receipts over five years.
• $57.6 million in additional government payments.
• $112.4 million net

That averages approximately $22.5 million annually.

These figures do not account for private compliance costs borne by exchanges and other providers, effects on competition and Bitcoin payments, or the wider privacy, cybersecurity and personal-safety risks.

They also do not identify how much revenue DCRR alone would raise, or why quarterly transaction-level reporting is preferable to less intrusive alternatives.

Collecting the data creates risks of its own.

Linking identities, home addresses and Bitcoin transaction records creates opportunities for unauthorised disclosure, extortion and physical targeting. 
Once exposed, that information cannot be recalled. Even outdated or incorrectly attributed records can put people and families at risk.

Security controls matter. But they do not answer whether the dataset should be created in the first place.

ABIB recommends removing Part 2 (DCRR) from the Exposure Draft.

Any domestic reporting regime should undergo separate policy assessment, legislative development and genuine public consultation.

We have asked Treasury to justify every proposed information field, demonstrate its additional value over existing collection, and explain why annual user-and-asset aggregates and targeted follow-up requests would be insufficient.

Investigative usefulness alone does not justify collecting every transfer or transaction identifier by default.

The consultation period is another concern.

After approximately 21 months between the close of the earlier consultation and this Exposure Draft, the public had just 13 days to examine a materially different reporting regime, with commencement proposed for 2027.

Laws affecting financial privacy, personal safety and Australian businesses deserve meaningful scrutiny.

Submissions close today, 28 October 2026.

We encourage individuals and businesses to make their views known:

posts.title: Second time this week the only working control in a financial crime story turns out to be Tether’s freeze button. Monday it was Iran’s central bank. Today it’s FinCEN’s review of 3
posts.author: Farnoush Mirmoeini
posts.snippet:
Second time this week the only working control in a financial crime story turns out to be Tether’s freeze button. Monday it was Iran’s central bank. Today it’s FinCEN’s review of 33,904 crypto scam reports, which shows where the one control against investment scams sits: with the stablecoin issuer at the end of the chain, and with nobody who files the reports.

The reflex after a report like this is to ask banks and exchanges for more monitoring. Every transaction in them was one the customer was entitled to make, and most filers saw only one phase. The one working control against crypto investment scams sits with the stablecoin issuer at the end of the chain, and with nobody who files the reports.

The reports tie about $12.7B of activity to these scams, and most filers saw one phase. Banks sit on the funding side, where a customer empties a retirement account or draws a home equity line to buy coins. Exchanges sit at the other end and watch a verified customer withdraw to an outside address.

Every leg of that route is a transaction the customer is entitled to make. The bank sees a transfer to a licensed exchange, into an account in the customer's own name. The exchange sees that customer buy coins and send them out. Monitoring is built to catch money leaving a customer without their say, or a third party pulling it out. Here the customer approves every step. The only step that reaches the scammer lands on a blockchain that no bank or exchange runs.

Scammers reuse the same collecting address for many victims, so an exchange can spot the pattern once a second or third customer sends money to it. By then the first ones have paid. The bank never sees the address at all.

When an institution does catch it early, it calls the customer, and the customer insists. The filings describe this over and over. In most, the bank or exchange raised it and then sent the money, because the instruction was valid and the money was theirs, and nothing in a license lets a firm refuse on a suspicion the customer has already heard and rejected.

Scam proceeds were swapped into stablecoins almost every time, nearly all of it into USDT. Tether can freeze an address and needs nobody's consent to do it. That is the control. It belongs to a company with no customer relationship, no refund obligation and no regulator asking it to use it, and everyone with a duty to the victim stands upstream of it, waiting for an address to repeat.
posts.reason: Deep analysis of stablecoin controls and crypto scam investment flows from FinCEN data invites expert forensic perspective and reaches compliance/regulatory audiences.

comments.text: The freeze-button point is right, but it understates the timing problem: by the time a filer identifies the collecting address, the issuer freeze only catches whatever hasn't already been swapped or bridged out — speed between first report and freeze request matters as much as the freeze capability itself.

Given that exchanges only see the pattern after a second or third victim sends to the same address, is there any proposal for cross-exchange address-sharing before the fact, rather than the current after-the-fact SAR pattern-matching?

In tracing work we routinely hit exactly this seam you describe — a fully 'authorised' transaction chain where every single hop looks legitimate to the institution handling it, and the only point where intent becomes visible is on-chain, after the money has already left.

posts.title: Investment Scams on WhatsApp and Telegram: A Warning Worth Taking Seriously
posts.author: Jeremy Andrews
posts.snippet:
Investment Scams on WhatsApp and Telegram: A Warning Worth Taking Seriously
How convincing online investment schemes can cost people their life savings — and what you can do to protect yourself.
At Meerkat Accountants, we believe that helping people make informed financial decisions extends beyond accounting and tax. We are increasingly concerned about investment and trading scams promoted through messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
These scams can be devastating. People are being persuaded to part with substantial sums of money, sometimes their entire life savings, through schemes that appear professional, credible and highly profitable.
The danger is that these are not always obvious get-rich-quick schemes. Scammers may use the names and branding of established investment firms, create convincing websites and trading platforms, and populate online groups with people claiming to have made substantial profits.
The objective is to gain your confidence and persuade you to invest.
How do these scams work?
The approach often follows a familiar pattern.
1. The invitation
You receive an unsolicited invitation to join a WhatsApp or Telegram group offering investment advice, trading tips or access to supposedly exclusive opportunities. You may never have expressed an interest in joining such a group.
2. Building confidence
The group appears professional. Administrators present themselves as investment experts, familiar company names may be used, and other members share apparently convincing accounts of their success.
But the testimonials, trading results and apparent profits may be entirely fabricated. Some of the people promoting the scheme may be working with the scammers.
3. The initial investment
You are encouraged to invest a relatively small amount. An online platform may display attractive profits, and you might even be allowed to withdraw a small sum to convince you that everything is genuine.
4. Increasing the stakes
Once your confidence has been established, you are encouraged to invest more. You may be told that a special opportunity is available for a limited time or that a larger investment will produce substantially better returns.
5. The trap closes
When you try to withdraw your money, problems suddenly arise. You may be asked to pay additional fees, tax, a security deposit or some other charge before your funds can be released.
You pay, but the money remains inaccessible. Eventually, the administrators disappear or stop responding.
The profits displayed on the platform may never have existed, and the money you transferred may already be gone.
To be continued

posts.author: James Crawshaw

Sometimes I really hate being proved right.

I've spoken about deepfakes quite a lot on here. And recently, at the TransUnion UK Summit, I even deepfaked one of our clients live in front of an audience, before explaining how I'd created it and how we can detect them.

One of the points I made then is the same one I'll make now. Deepfakes can be easier to defend against than you might think. They're generally designed to fool humans, not specialist detection systems.

Which is why I've always said that, of all the ways deepfakes can be used for fraud, social engineering worries me the most.

Because in that scenario, fooling a human is precisely the point.

And unfortunately, new figures from Report Fraud rather reinforce that concern.

£24.3 million lost in just eight months, across more than 1,300 reports of AI-enabled investment endorsement scams.

Fake celebrity endorsements, convincing videos and apparently trustworthy investment opportunities. All designed to persuade somebody to hand over their money.

And whilst we can build increasingly sophisticated technology to detect synthetic media, there's no guarantee the person watching a convincing video on Facebook has those defences available.

But please don't take this as me saying we should never trust anything again, or that the world's fake and we're all just living in it.

Because the advice is remarkably similar to what it's been since fraud first became a thing.

Take your time. Double-check through an independent source. Don't let somebody rush you into handing over money.

And if something sounds too good to be true...

Well, I hate to say it.

Money market fund and investor platforms are seemingly a hot cake for sharp boys.

I have seen 3 so far imitating ziidi trader by Safaricom PLC. I have also seen one imitating Etica Capital Ltd.

So this is what happens. The scammer creates a clone website of the real platform, juicy investment returns to lure in people and then when you invest, they swallow your money like those small ripe banana. Mzima mzima.

So what can the real platforms do.

1. Identify the scam domain name registrants and hosting companies. For example, 2 websites mimicking ziidi were registered on namecheap and hosted by the same. 


It is easy to identify these details by checking the WHOIS information.

Once you have this information, write to the abuse department of the domain registrant/hosting.

In the screenshot attached for example, I would write to abuse[at]name[dot]com

Say for example that people were googling "etica money market fund" or "ziidi trader" and search engines would have the scam site leading infront of the real platform.

Honestly, this step takes time for Google to act.

I would advise to try step 1 first. Once the site is down, Google will derank the site on finding it does not exist

Un finto colloquio di lavoro ha infettato 30.000 computer in oltre 100 Paesi.

Qualche settimana fa l’FBI, la polizia giapponese e le agenzie di intelligence di Australia e Germania hanno pubblicato un avviso congiunto su WaterPlum, un gruppo legato alla Corea del Nord. La campagna si chiama Contagious Interview. E il nome, da solo, basta quasi a spiegare tutto.

Lo schema è questo:
→ finti recruiter, spesso presentati come aziende reali del mondo AI, crypto o NFT.
→ primo contatto su social, job board e piattaforme freelance.
→ colloquio tecnico, poi la richiesta: “scarica questo file per il coding test.”
→ dentro quel file c’è un malware che ruba password, wallet e documenti d’identità. 

Il bilancio: oltre 7.000 wallet svuotati e circa 10,7 milioni di dollari finiti a Pyongyang.

posts.title: Germany wants to freeze accounts and safe deposit boxes in days. Here is what changes.
posts.author: Michael (Mica) Mayenberg
posts.snippet:
Germany wants to freeze accounts and safe deposit boxes in days. Here is what changes.

Germany's finance ministry (Lars Klingbeil, SPD) has a draft law against money laundering.
 
According to BILD, it implements new EU rules. It is a draft, not law yet.
The key points:

1. Faster freezes. The financial intelligence unit could stop suspicious money flows with an immediate measure of up to 10 working days. Accounts and other financial transactions could be restricted temporarily.

2. Safe deposit boxes. In certain cases, access could be blocked for up to 5 working days.

3. A central property register. Land, owners, beneficial owners (the people who really own or control a company) and purchase prices would be bundled in one place and accessible to authorities electronically. Planned start: July 2029.

4. More account access. The account retrieval system would also cover crypto accounts and accounts with virtual IBANs. EU account registers would be linked, so authorities can see accounts in other member states more easily.

5. Cash limit. Commercial cash payments capped at 10,000 euros across the EU. Private payments between individuals are not covered.

6. Stronger checks on companies, including on-site checks of ownership data, and higher fines.

Most rules would apply from July 2027. The ministry expects about 1.6 million euros of extra yearly cost for businesses.

For ordinary salary and bills, the draft creates no new duties. The data does not become public. Whether everything comes exactly like this is still open.

My take:

Fighting money laundering is a fair goal. Nobody should argue against that.

But one thing is clear: the direction is MORE connected data. Accounts, crypto, property and ownership across countries, visible to authorities in one picture.

So here is the question for everyone with assets in more than one country:

Can you list every account, wallet, property and company stake you hold, in every country, today? Most people cannot. And an incomplete picture is a risk: for taxes, for compliance, for your own peace of mind.

posts.title: Back online ends the outage. Under HIPAA, it does not close the incident.
posts.author: Mwendwa Wachira
posts.snippet:
Back online ends the outage. Under HIPAA, it does not close the incident.

On Monday, October 26, #UNM Health Sciences began containing a cybersecurity threat around 11 a.m. Ambulances were temporarily diverted, outpatient surgeries and appointments were suspended for the day and systems came back in phases from 2:30 p.m. By Tuesday, UNM said critical systems were back online and the event affected some end-user devices but not core systems or servers. By Wednesday, clinical operations were fully functional.

That is a fast recovery.

The important point is not how quickly the screens came back. It is what an organization can show about the hours in between.

Under 45 CFR 164.308(a)(7), a #HIPAA contingency plan includes data backup, disaster recovery and emergency mode operation plans (all required). Testing and revision and a criticality analysis are addressable: you decide how to meet them based on your size, systems, costs and #risk analysis and document that decision.

In my view, emergency mode deserves the most attention: it must keep critical processes running while still protecting ePHI. Under 164.308(a)(6), the organization must respond to the incident, mitigate harmful effects where practicable and document the #incident and its outcome.

For a COO or practice administrator, I would examine three things after any downtime:
a) Emergency mode - Which critical processes kept running and how was patient information protected on paper forms, local workstations and shared devices?
b) Restoration evidence. Proof that restored systems and data were verified as complete and accurate, not just reachable. OCR’s #ransomware guidance recommends periodic test restorations for this reason.
c) The incident file. A dated record of what happened, who owned each step and the breach determination. Under 164.402, an impermissible access, acquisition, use or disclosure of PHI is presumed a breach unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise.

My decision rule: I would not close a downtime event until the file answers all three and the lessons have reached the risk analysis and the contingency plan.

This does not mean UNM Health had a #breach or a #compliance failure. UNM says core systems were not reached and the investigation is ongoing. Not every security incident is a breach.

#HHS has proposed requiring restoration within 72 hours. That is not yet law but it signals that restoration will be measured not assumed.

The objective is not simply to come back online. It is to show how patient information was protected while you were offline.

Before your next downtime #drill, test whether your team can produce those three records.

Side note:
* A periodic test restoration means taking data from your backups and restoring it on a schedule, before anything goes wrong. It shows whether the backups actually work. *
posts.reason: HIPAA incident response and forensics by a healthcare security professional targeting compliance officers and risk managers, with technical depth that signals relevance to our AML and NIS2 audience.

comments.text: The distinction you draw between reachable and verified-accurate restoration is the one most incident reports gloss over - we regularly see organisations declare systems 'back online' without a documented test restoration confirming data integrity, which becomes a real liability under 164.308(a)(7) if it's ever examined.

On the incident file point - in your experience, how often does the documented risk assessment under 164.402 actually get built contemporaneously during the response, versus reconstructed afterward under pressure from counsel?

In ransomware-adjacent cases we've supported, the gap between operational recovery and a defensible incident file is almost always where organisations get caught out later - the forensic record needs the same rigor as the technical containment.

From online banking and social media to cloud computing and artificial intelligence, we depend on digital platforms more than ever. Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, applications, and sensitive information from cyberattacks. Threats such as phishing, ransomware, identity theft, and data breaches can affect individuals, businesses, and even governments.

One of the biggest misconceptions is that cyberattacks target only large organizations. In reality, anyone using the internet can become a victim. Simple habits, such as using strong and unique passwords, enabling multi-factor authentication, avoiding suspicious links, and regularly updating software, can significantly improve online security.

As technology continues to evolve, cybersecurity is no longer just a technical responsibility. It is a shared responsibility that requires awareness, continuous learning, and proactive action from everyone.

For students and aspiring professionals, cybersecurity offers exciting opportunities to learn, innovate, and contribute to a safer digital environment. Developing skills in network security, ethical hacking, threat detection, and risk management can help build a strong foundation for a career in this field.

I believe that creating a secure digital future begins with awareness today. By staying informed, adopting safe online practices, and encouraging others to do the same, we can collectively make the internet a safer place.

Understanding Money Laundering: A Brief Guide 🏦💰

This image is an educational infographic from the "Urdu Dictionary" explaining the concept of Money Laundering in simple terms. Here is a breakdown of what is written on the page:

Title:
Money Laundering
("Money Laundering" Kese Kehte Hain?) - What is called Money Laundering?

Definition (تعریف):
Money laundering is an illegal legal process through which illegal funds (Black Money) are made to appear as clean/halal money (White Money).

Three Common Stages of Money Laundering:

The infographic outlines that money laundering usually happens in three stages:

1. Placement (Placing): The illegal money is first introduced into the financial system or banking system. It is mixed with legal money and deposited into banks.

2. Layering (Layering): To hide the true source of the money, complex transactions are created. This involves moving money through various bank accounts, companies, or different countries, making it extremely difficult to trace.

3. Integration (Integration): The money is brought back into the mainstream economy in a way that it appears to be completely legal property and legitimate profit.

Footer:
Urdu Dictionary

Reflection & Reminder (Islamic Perspective)

While this image is a financial/legal definition, the concept of keeping our earnings pure is deeply rooted in Islamic teachings. Islam places immense emphasis on Halal (permissible) and Haram (forbidden) wealth.

Here are some important Islamic principles related to this topic:

1. The Obligation of Halal Earnings:
Islam commands Muslims to earn wealth through legitimate means and strictly forbids earning through deception, theft, bribery, or interest (Riba).

The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) said:
"The feet of a son of Adam will not move from near his Lord on the Day of Judgment until he is asked about five things: about his life and how he lived it, about his youth and how he utilized it, about his wealth: where he earned it from and how he spent it..."
(Jami` at-Tirmidhi, Hadith 2416 - Hasan)

2. The Consequence of Unlawful Wealth:
Money acquired through illegal means (black money) does not bring true blessing (barakah). It is considered a form of oppression and corruption on earth.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said:
"Any body that is nourished by unlawful means will not enter Paradise."
(Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 2076)

3. A Reminder Regarding Riba:
The third stage of money laundering often involves complex financial structures that may include Riba (interest). Islam strongly warns against this.

Allah says in the Qur'an:
"O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains [due to you] of interest, if you are indeed believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war [against you] from Allah and His Messenger."
(Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:278-279)

On October 28, Seva Nivesh organized an event bringing together philanthropists for a conversation on catalytic finance, an approach that can help philanthropic capital go further by using it to unlock additional resources and opportunities.

The session began with Harshu Ghate introducing the funding challenges faced by nonprofits, including the need to diversify funding sources. 
Our guest speaker, Priya Naik, founder of Samhita , then shared how Samhita-CGF is using catalytic finance to address barriers to financial inclusion and livelihood opportunities.

Catalytic finance is about making a given amount of funding do more. For example, a returnable grant provides flexible capital for a livelihood or enterprise, with repayment adjusted to the recipient's financial circumstances so the funds can be recycled to support others.

Priya shared the methods and the impact of their initiatives, with examples of women entrepreneurs who used these grants to strengthen their businesses and improve their livelihoods. 

The event highlighted an important principle. Philanthropic capital can do more than fund an immediate need. It can help unlock other sources of capital, test new approaches, and create pathways for people to access further opportunities.

An obvious question for philanthropists was how do we get to participate in such funding with a multiplier effect? The 𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱 (SIF) set up by Seva Nivesh provides the answer. Individual philanthropists can contribute to the Fund and the pooled funds will be invested as catalytic capital in livelihood projects. 

At Seva Nivesh, we see value in bringing these conversations to the forefront, helping the social sector understand emerging funding approaches and explore how they might apply them to their own work.

We appreciate Priya Naik for sharing her experience of how these approaches can support people and livelihoods.

posts.title: Ahh, data centers… the new battle ground!
posts.author: Ramon Garcia
posts.snippet:
Ahh, data centers… the new battle ground!

Not all data centers have the same environmental footprint. Treating them as though they do misrepresents an entire industry.

Communities deserve clear answers about a facility’s design, location, and operations. Let’s address common concerns:

🔊 “Data centers bring noise to our neighborhoods.”
Disruptive noise is not inevitable. Appropriate locations, setbacks, quieter equipment, acoustic enclosures, and enforceable sound limits can reduce neighborhood impacts. Sound assessments should include low-frequency noise.

🏗️ “Data centers offer no benefit to the local economy.”
Construction, skilled operating positions, local service contracts, and tax revenue are tangible benefits. Permanent staffing may be modest, and incentives affect the public return. Evaluate each project’s commitments.

⚡ “Data centers will drain our power.”
Demand can be substantial, making capacity planning essential. Responsible projects should demonstrate adequate supply, fund their fair share of infrastructure upgrades, and protect existing customers from unfair cost increases.

☀️ “Data centers can’t operate more sustainably.”
Solar, wind, geothermal, and other suitable resources can help supply operations and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Onsite generation and contracts supporting new clean-energy projects can contribute to that supply.

Battery storage can shift solar and wind energy to other hours and manage peak demand. Where conditions permit, outdoor-air cooling and ground-source cooling can reduce mechanical cooling needs. Captured waste heat can serve buildings or industrial processes.

These options depend on location and engineering. Solar and wind vary with weather and time, so reliable operation still requires a coordinated mix of generation, storage, and grid capacity. Annual renewable-energy matching alone does not mean a facility runs on clean power every hour.

💧 “Data centers destroy our water resources.”
Water demand varies by cooling technology and climate. Dry cooling can sharply reduce direct cooling-water consumption, while reclaimed water may reduce demand on drinking-water supplies. Energy and water tradeoffs should be evaluated together.

🌱 “Data centers kill people, animals, plants, and jobs.”
That sweeping claim requires project-specific evidence. Responsible development should address emissions, habitat, stormwater, water availability, and community health through measurable safeguards and ongoing monitoring.

Supporting digital infrastructure and protecting the environment are compatible goals.

The standard should be clear: appropriate sites, efficient design, responsible energy and water use, transparent reporting, enforceable protections, and meaningful community benefits.

Judge each project by its evidence, engineering, and accountability. Responsible developers should welcome that scrutiny.

Spiegare Consulting annual policy pilgrimage took place this month with Jane O'Dwyer from Cooperative Research Australia and my colleague Dr Faisal Younus joining me to discuss the 2026 National Innovation Policy Forum and Built Here Parliamentary Showcase held in Canberra this month.

Reinforcing to politicians the importance of innovation as an underlying driver for improved productivity and economic outcomes was seen as critical in maintaining momentum for investment in the innovation system. Faisal reflected on the showcase and noted that ‘built here’ needed to include opportunities for regional and rural Australia to move beyond raw material sources to more value-added industries. Jane noted that the showcase reinforced that we can build industries and companies and the full potential of the innovation system was on display.

We spent a little time reprising the nexus between innovation and economic outcomes, the role of central agencies, and the need for policy and political leadership to recognise the connection. Jane expressed the hope that the National Resilience and Science Council, led by the Prime Minister, will drive action. Faisal reflected on the need to challenge the definitions of success in the innovation system, and how innovation meets paying customers and generates export revenue. In part, this is also around the role of government as a customer and how procurement policy changes (raised by David Forman from TechnologyOne a few years back) still need adjusting to at least level the procurement playing field! We cannot continue to invest public funds into technology development and then be surprised when they go offshore for customers.

Jane reinforced that this theme has emerged at all previous forums and at all the tables on the day, noting this is also discussed in the halls of parliament around who is buying the resulting products from the domestic innovation system. We touched on Magellan Power and Gap Drone as contrasting examples of where government creates markets.

Faisal introduced the question of choices and where we might choose to lead or actively choose to stop funding. Related to the concept of choice, Aaron Violi MP, Shadow Minister for the Science, Technology and Innovation, touched on the global competition for capital and talent. We then had a discussion inspired by Anton Middelberg FTSE FNAI around systems, and systems within systems! The government’s ambitions were summarised by Tim Ayres, Minister for Industry and Innovation, and Minister for Science.

Our final reflection was taken from Sophia Hamblin Wang, Shannon Willoughby and Roy Green, raising the question of how to make the innovation system as part of the voter calculus at the next election.

Ten times the container capacity starts in factories that do not exist yet.

On 28 October, the Union Cabinet approved the Container Manufacturing Promotion Scheme, with a total outlay of approx Rs 10,000 crore utilised through FY 2039-40. Reported aim: raise domestic container manufacturing capacity roughly ten-fold, from approx 70,000 TEUs per year to approx 7.5 lakh TEUs per year, through support for greenfield projects of at least 1,00,000 TEUs and brownfield expansions of at least 25,000 TEUs.

As reported, not independently verified: approved projects, fund allocations per project, implementation timelines and expected hiring not disclosed in the announcements.

Technical: approving an outlay is not capacity. Approx 7.5 lakh TEUs per year has to be built as factories, lines and supply chains, project by project, and the 1,00,000 TEU greenfield floor and 25,000 TEU brownfield floor concentrate proposals into large, capital-intensive builds.

Workforce: panel fabrication, corrugation and container assembly trades; welding engineers for high-rate steel lines; greenfield plant engineering across layout, material flow, paint and testing lines; container certification and structural QA/QC; programme and procurement teams holding steel feed and phased capacity targets together.

On a ten-fold container capacity ramp, where does your bench strain first: fabrication trades, plant setup or certification throughput?

I am sharing my recent podcast in the series of #Zhonghua Mundus by Bruegel - Improving economic policy.
For roughly two decades, #China's local governments used the revenue from selling land to property developers to build roads, metro lines and new urban districts, and to cover a large share of their spending. But when the property market slumped, developers began to default and land sales fell sharply, leaving localities with heavy debts and a shrinking source of revenue.
In this episode, Yuyun Zhan and I welcome Tianlei Huang to discuss the problem. We explored how China’s land finance model helped fund the country’s economic development and why it could not last. With no single source able to replace the vast revenue from land sales, deep structural reform will be needed to stabilise local government finances.

posts.snippet:
KHÔNG CÓ THÂN NHÂN BẢO LÃNH: 3 CON ĐƯỜNG ĐỊNH CƯ MỸ AN TOÀN NHẤT
---------------------------------------------------
Nhiều người lầm tưởng muốn định cư Mỹ bắt buộc phải có người thân (bố mẹ, anh chị em, vợ/chồng) bảo lãnh. Trên thực tế, Luật Di trú Mỹ dành riêng nhóm diện EB (Employment-Based - Định cư dựa trên Đầu tư & Lao động) cho những cá nhân độc lập hoàn toàn, không có bất kỳ mối quan hệ thân nhân nào tại Mỹ.

1️⃣ EB-5 (Đầu Tư Trực Tiếp / Quỹ Trung Tâm Cấp Vùng)
- Đối tượng: Nhà đầu tư độc lập có nguồn vốn khả dụng. Không phụ thuộc vào người thân hay chủ lao động.
- Bản chất: Tài chính đổi lấy Thẻ xanh vĩnh viễn. Bạn dùng vốn của mình để tạo ra 10 việc làm cho lao động Mỹ.
- Điều kiện cốt lõi:
Chi trả $800,000 USD vào dự án thuộc khu vực TEA (Nông thôn)
Chứng minh Nguồn tiền hợp pháp (Source of Funds).
- Thời gian xử lý: 1.5 – 2.5 năm (Dự án Nông thôn - Rural TEA được ưu tiên xét duyệt siêu tốc).
- Điểm mạnh: Chủ động 100%, cấp Thẻ xanh cho cả gia đình (Vợ/chồng và con dưới 21 tuổi).

2️⃣ EB-3 Skilled Workers (Diện Tay Nghề / Chuyên Gia)
- Đối tượng: Lao động có bằng Cử nhân hoặc tối thiểu 2 năm kinh nghiệm/đào tạo (thợ cơ khí, đầu bếp, kỹ thuật viên, kế toán, IT...).
- Bản chất: Chuyên môn đổi lấy Thẻ xanh. Một doanh nghiệp tại Mỹ đứng ra bảo lãnh vị trí làm việc cho bạn.
- Điều kiện cốt lõi:
=> Có Job Offer hợp pháp từ Doanh nghiệp Mỹ.

posts.title: If VAT ever got its own drama series, the reverse charge mechanism (RCM) would deserve a few episodes, if not a full season. It has everything a good script needs: heroes, villains
posts.author: Sorin Biban
posts.snippet:
If VAT ever got its own drama series, the reverse charge mechanism (RCM) would deserve a few episodes, if not a full season. It has everything a good script needs: heroes, villains, complicated relationships – and a cliffhanger every few years.

 👉 In a resolution of 20 October 2026 on combating VAT fraud, the European Parliament (i) acknowledged that the optional RCM provided for in Articles 199a and 199b of the VAT Directive has proved clearly effective as an anti-fraud instrument, by removing the structural opportunity for missing traders, and (ii) called on the Commission to propose not only extending Articles 199a and 199b beyond 2026, but also broadening their scope.

 👉 The resolution came just weeks after the Commission had published, on 1 October 2026, a proposal for a Council Directive to extend the optional RCM (Article 199a) and the Quick Reaction Mechanism (Article 199b) until 30 June 2030. The proposal only moves the current end date of 31 December 2026; it leaves the scope untouched. The extension until 30 June 2030 is meant as a transitional measure until the start of the Digital Reporting Requirements (DRR) under the ViDA package, including the so-called central VIES, a new centralised hub for cross-border reporting and taxpayer identification.

 👉 Shortly after the proposal was published, three Member States (Austria, Czechia and Germany) asked for the scope of Article 199a to be widened to cover certain real estate transactions, motor vehicles, national greenhouse gas emission allowances and certain transactions paid for with crypto-assets.

 👉 Earlier, on 2 June 2026, at a public hearing of the European Parliament’s Subcommittee on Tax Matters (FISC), the experts’ verdict was far from enthusiastic. Besides flagging its risks and weaknesses, they noted that the RCM is not in itself the solution to VAT fraud. The real praise went to ViDA’s Digital Reporting Requirements.

It remains to be seen whether, and in what form, the RCM will survive beyond 30 June 2030, once ViDA’s DRR become applicable.

As a CySEC-authorised Crypto-Asset Service Provider under MiCA, Collect & Exchange  (collectnexchange.cy) supports businesses exploring crypto payment acceptance and crypto-to-fiat conversion.

💡 My takeaway: Crypto adoption becomes meaningful when it solves a real business problem.

💡 My takeaway: FinTech competition is increasingly about building connected financial ecosystems.

💡 My takeaway: Digital assets are becoming part of broader financial service strategies.

FinTech isn't moving in just one direction.

posts.title: En direct à la télévision, sur AL24 News, ce matin : la fraude au président n’a pas attendu l’IA. Le deepfake lui prête une voix et un visage.
posts.author: Mehdi Labbani
posts.snippet:
En direct à la télévision, sur AL24 News, ce matin : la fraude au président n’a pas attendu l’IA. Le deepfake lui prête une voix et un visage.

Jeudi 29 octobre, j’y suis intervenu de nouveau, en visioconférence, dans la matinale : un format où la confiance repose justement sur un visage et une voix.

Un client s’authentifie parfaitement, puis valide lui-même un virement demandé par un faux conseiller, soi-disant pour « annuler une opération suspecte ». Aucune faille informatique : une voix de confiance, un contexte crédible, et l’argent part.

Ma conviction : reconnaître une voix ou un visage ne prouve plus rien. Inutile de prouver qu’une voix est fausse : il suffit de vérifier la demande.

𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗲̀𝗿𝗲𝘀 :
→ En France, les fraudes par manipulation pèsent environ 40 % des montants fraudés au premier semestre 2025, contre 32 % en 2023 et 2024 (Banque de France).
→ En 2024, un employé du cabinet Arup, à Hong Kong, a viré environ 25 M$ après une visio où tous les participants étaient des deepfakes.
→ À l’inverse, un responsable de site français, visé par un faux dirigeant en visio, a mis fin à l’échange et alerté sa direction (cas relayé par la DGSI).

Je l’ai observé auprès de trésoriers, et vécu moi-même : à plusieurs reprises, de faux services du monde crypto m’ont appelé pour « vérifier une opération ». Bien souvent, c’étaient des tentatives d’attaque. Le réflexe qui protège : raccrocher, puis contacter soi-même le service client de la plateforme par son canal officiel.

Je travaille avec des banques et des fintechs sur les paiements et les actifs numériques. La détection n’est qu’un maillon : le risque se joue dans la chaîne d’autorisation.

Trois questions avant toute opération sensible :
→ Qui demande, et par quel canal ?
→ L’ai-je confirmé par un second canal, choisi par moi ?
→ Pourra-t-on revenir en arrière ?

La troisième pèse encore plus avec le paiement instantané et les actifs numériques : le règlement est définitif, donc le contrôle doit précéder l’exécution.

Je conseille aussi des trésoriers qui s’orientent vers le paiement agentique, avec le même message : avant de confier des paiements à un agent IA, vérifier l’authenticité de chaque partie (KYC), puis établir qui fait quoi et selon quelle procédure. Avec le paiement instantané : qui paie, comment, et comment être sûr de ne pas se faire avoir.

Aucun détecteur n’est infaillible : une performance annoncée se juge en conditions réelles. Pour les startups deeptech et les jeunes ingénieurs en IA, le terrain est ouvert : nouvelles manipulations, parcours d’identité, fausses alertes. Une banque adopte ce qui est robuste et s’intègre à ses parcours.

Merci à l’équipe d’ AL24news - قناة الجزائر الدولية pour cet échange en direct.

𝗠𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲́ : la confirmation indépendante avant toute opération irréversible. Si la demande venait de votre directeur, en visio, votre équipe appliquerait-elle ces trois questions ?

posts.title: Operators with a valid gaming license still get rejected by banks and PSPs. The licence is the regulator’s decision; the bank or PSP runs its own risk assessment, and for iGaming i
posts.author: Anatolii Liubich
posts.snippet:
Operators with a valid gaming license still get rejected by banks and PSPs. The licence is the regulator’s decision; the bank or PSP runs its own risk assessment, and for iGaming it is one of the strictest in payments. Gambling transactions sit under MCC 7995, which card schemes classify as high-risk, so the acquirer carries the operator’s risk on its own books.

What they look at before onboarding:
1. Licence and target markets. Which regulator issued the licence, and whether you accept players only where you’re allowed to. Weak geo-blocking is one of the fastest routes to a rejection.
2. Ownership. Full UBO structure, source of funds and source of wealth for the owners, and the history of every entity in the group.
3. AML programme. Player KYC, risk scoring, transaction monitoring, the SAR process, and an MLRO who can answer questions on a call.
4. Responsible gaming. Deposit limits, self-exclusion, and affordability checks where the market requires them.
5. Flow of funds. How player money moves, where it is held, how withdrawals work, and who else touches it: affiliates, payment agents, crypto on-ramps.
6. Numbers. Expected volumes, chargeback and fraud ratios, refund rates. Projections that don’t match the business model raise more questions than low volumes do.

Most rejections we see come from an application that leaves these questions unanswered, while the licence itself is in order.

Complywiser helps operators prepare banking and PSP applications and find partners that onboard iGaming.
